title: McArdle Disease Heterozygotes and Toe Walking Onset in children: A Cohort Study on Genotype and Phenotype Interplay
summary:
What is this study about?
This study looked at whether changes in the PYGM gene (linked to a rare muscle disorder called McArdle disease) might explain why some children walk on their toes for longer than usual. Normally, McArdle disease only occurs when a child inherits two faulty copies of the gene – but this research focused on children with just one faulty copy, who were previously thought to be healthy.
 What did the researchers do?
     - Used advanced genetic testing (Next-Generation Sequencing)
     - Analyzed clinical symptoms in 71 PYGM mutation positive children who persistently walked on their toes (with no neurological or orthopedic cause)
      - Tracked symptoms like high foot arches, muscle pain, cramps, and tiredness

Key Findings:

    Surprising Symptoms in "Healthy" Carriers:
      - 93% of children had high foot arches (pes cavus)
      - muscle pain or tiring easily during exercise, and cramps were reported 
      - A single faulty PYGM gene copy – previously considered harmless – may cause toe walking and other symptoms in children.

Why This Matters:
- Earlier Diagnosis: Toe walking + high arches could be a sign to check for metabolic issues
- Better Care: Affected children might benefit from tailored exercises or diet adjustments
- New Understanding: Overturns the assumption that carriers with one faulty gene copy stay healthy

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Zehenspitzengang mehr als die Hälfte des Tages 
Absolvieren eines spezifischen Gentests mit einem Panel von 49 Genen
Exclusion criteria:
Prescence of neurological/orthopedic conditions, such as cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder, tethered cord syndrome, children with birth complications, severe orthopedic deformities including limb length discrepancies, scoliosis or severe foot deformities.
